title: Variable Lifetime
body:
**When** a variable's storage exists. A run-time question, and a different one from
[[Variable Scope]], which asks where the *name* is visible.

Three lifetimes in C++:

| Lifetime | Created | Destroyed | Lives on |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Automatic** (the default local) | when the block is entered | when the block exits | the stack |
| **Static** | before `main()` starts | when the program ends | a fixed area |
| **Dynamic** | when you call `new` | when you call `delete` | the heap |

```c++
void f() {
	int a = 0;           // automatic: new one every call
	static int b = 0;    // static: one, forever, initialised once
	int *c = new int;    // dynamic: yours until you delete it
	a++; b++;
	cout << a << " " << b;   // 1 1, then 1 2, then 1 3, ...
}
```

`b` is the case that separates lifetime from scope cleanly: it is **out of scope** between
calls (nothing outside `f` can name it) and **alive** the whole time.

The two failures at the ends of this table are the reason it matters:

- **Returning a pointer to a local.** The automatic variable dies at the `}`, so the caller
  holds an address of memory that has been handed back. A dangling pointer, and it usually
  does not crash, which makes it worse. See [[Runtime Errors]].
- **Never calling `delete`.** Dynamic storage has no automatic end, so it stays allocated
  after the last [[Pointer]] to it is gone. A memory leak. See [[new And delete]].

Automatic lifetime is the one you get for free and it is why local variables are safe:
allocation and deallocation are the stack pointer moving, which costs nothing and cannot be
forgotten. Everything about that mechanism is in [[Stack and Heap]], and how the machine
actually does it is [[Subroutines]] in [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]].

[[Storage Class]] is the C++ keyword that selects between the first two.
